A sacrament is a sacred religious ritual or ceremony in which a physical, visible action is believed to carry a spiritual reality — either symbolising God's grace, delivering it directly, or both. Think of it as a moment where the physical world and the spiritual world touch each other in a formally defined, deliberate way.

The most famous classical definition of a sacrament (which still guides most Christian thinking today) is: "an outward and visible sign of an inward and spiritual grace." Break that down:

  • Outward and visible — something you can see happening in the physical world: water being poured, bread being eaten, oil being applied.
  • Inward and spiritual grace — something happening in the soul or spirit that cannot be seen: forgiveness, divine blessing, entry into God's community, spiritual strengthening.

So a sacrament is not just a ceremony for ceremony's sake. It is meant to accomplish or represent something real and profound — an encounter between the human and the divine.
Where the Word Is Most Commonly Used

The word "sacrament" belongs primarily to Christian theology and practice, though it can appear in a broader sense too (more on that at the end).

In Christianity, different denominations disagree quite significantly on sacraments — specifically on how many there are, what they do, and how they work. These disagreements are some of the most important divisions in Christian history.
What a Sacrament Is Supposed to Do

This is the central debate, and understanding it will help you understand everything else about the word.

View 1 — Sacraments actually deliver grace (Catholic and Orthodox position):
In this view, when a sacrament is performed correctly and by the right person, it doesn't just point to grace — it gives it. The act itself is the channel. This is sometimes called ex opere operato, a Latin phrase meaning "by the work done." Just as a pipe delivers water regardless of whether the plumber who installed it is a good or bad person, a sacrament delivers grace by virtue of the act itself, not by the worthiness of the priest or the recipient. The recipient needs to be open and not actively blocking it, but the sacrament does real, objective spiritual work.

View 2 — Sacraments are signs and seals that strengthen faith (mainstream Protestant position):
Here, sacraments don't work mechanically. Grace comes through faith, not through the physical act. The sacrament is a visible promise from God — it confirms and seals what is received through faith, like an official stamp on a document. It strengthens and nourishes the believer's faith but doesn't operate independently of it.

View 3 — Sacraments are purely symbolic memorials (some Protestant traditions):
In this view, a sacrament is simply a memorial or reminder — an act of remembrance and public declaration. When Christians eat bread and drink wine together, for instance, they are simply remembering Christ's sacrifice and declaring their faith publicly. No grace is delivered by the act itself; it is entirely a human act of commemoration.

Both Roman Catholicism and Eastern Orthodoxy recognise seven sacraments, all believed to have been instituted by Jesus Christ either directly or through the apostles:

1. Baptism
Water is poured over, sprinkled on, or the person is fully immersed in water, in the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. This marks entry into the Christian community, symbolises cleansing from sin (Catholics believe it removes original sin — the inherited sinful nature of humanity), and is seen as a spiritual rebirth. It is unrepeatable.

2. The Eucharist (also called Holy Communion or the Lord's Supper)
Bread and wine are consecrated and shared. Catholics hold the doctrine of transubstantiation — the belief that the bread and wine literally become the body and blood of Jesus Christ during the Mass, even though they continue to look, taste, and smell the same. This is not mere symbolism in Catholic teaching; Christ is truly and fully present. The Eucharist is considered the central and most important of all the sacraments.

3. Confirmation (called Chrismation in Orthodoxy)
The gifts of the Holy Spirit, received at baptism, are strengthened and "confirmed." In Catholicism, it is typically administered by a bishop using holy oil (chrism), who anoints the forehead of the recipient. In Orthodoxy, Chrismation is performed immediately after baptism (even for infants), anointing various parts of the body with oil.

4. Penance (Confession or Reconciliation)
The person confesses their sins to a priest, expresses genuine sorrow, and receives absolution — a formal pronouncement of forgiveness spoken by the priest on behalf of God. A penance (a prayer or act) is usually assigned. Catholics believe the priest is acting as an instrument through which God grants forgiveness, not forgiving in his own name.

5. Anointing of the Sick (formerly called Extreme Unction or Last Rites)
Holy oil is applied to a person who is seriously ill or in danger of death. It is believed to bring spiritual healing, strengthen the person against spiritual danger, and sometimes physical healing too. It also prepares the soul for death and can include the forgiveness of sins.

6. Holy Orders (Ordination)
The sacrament by which men are ordained as deacons, priests, or bishops. It is believed to confer a permanent spiritual mark on the recipient and the authority to act in the person of Christ — especially to celebrate the Eucharist and grant absolution. This sacrament is not available to women in Catholicism or Orthodoxy, though this is a subject of significant debate.

7. Matrimony (Marriage)
In Catholic teaching, marriage between two baptised Christians is itself a sacrament. The couple are considered to administer the sacrament to each other by giving their free, full, and lifelong consent. Marriage is understood as an unbreakable covenant that mirrors the relationship between Christ and the Church.

Most Protestant denominations recognise only two sacraments — specifically the ones Jesus is recorded as directly instituting in the New Testament:

1. Baptism — directly commanded by Jesus ("Go and make disciples of all nations, baptising them...")

2. The Lord's Supper (Eucharist/Communion) — directly instituted by Jesus at the Last Supper ("Do this in remembrance of me.")

The other five are considered important rites or ceremonies (sometimes called ordinances) but not true sacraments in the strict sense, because they were not explicitly instituted by Jesus himself with a physical sign and a promise attached.

It's worth noting that even among Protestants, there is substantial disagreement about these two. For example:

  • Lutherans believe in the "real presence" of Christ in the bread and wine — not transubstantiation, but Christ is truly present with, in, and under the elements.
  • Calvinists/Reformed believe Christ is spiritually but truly present in the Eucharist for those who receive it in faith.
  • Zwinglians and many Baptists believe the Lord's Supper is a purely symbolic memorial.

Some Christian groups, notably the Quakers (Religious Society of Friends) and the Salvation Army, practise no sacraments at all. Their reasoning: all of life is sacred, and no particular ritual holds special status above another. External ceremonies are seen as unnecessary or even distracting from inward, spiritual faith.

Outside its specifically Christian theological meaning, "sacrament" is used in a metaphorical or secular sense to describe any act or ritual that is treated with the deepest reverence and solemnity — as though it were holy or untouchable.

For example:

  • "For this family, Sunday dinner was a sacrament — no one ever missed it, and no distraction was allowed."
  • "He treated the craft of writing as a sacrament."

In this broader usage, the word conveys that something is not merely routine or habitual, but is approached with a kind of sacred gravity and meaning. It suggests the act connects the person to something larger than themselves.
A Quick Summary to Tie It All Together

A sacrament is a formal, sacred ritual in which something physically visible (water, bread, oil, the spoken word) is used as a vehicle or sign for something spiritually significant (forgiveness, grace, entry into a community of faith, divine blessing). The main questions surrounding the word are: how many sacraments are there?, what exactly do they accomplish?, and how do they work? — and different Christian traditions answer these questions very differently. Outside religion, the word can describe any deeply solemn, reverential ritual that holds profound meaning for the person or group performing it.
